  "chapter_body_excerpt": "# 6 Replenish or attack? Competing etiologies and therapies of madness in Ming medicine When there is depletion, replenish it; when there is repletion: drain it. 虛者補之 實者瀉之 Canon of Problems 難經, problem 69 This chapter explains the rich developments that took place in elite medical thinking and practice from roughly 1530 to 1650. In addition to writing long sections on diankuang in their treatises, physicians from this ebullient period recorded in some detail how they handled specific cases of madness. All of these men had read the Danxi xinfa 丹溪心法 (1482), knew of Wang Lun's 王綸 (1453-1510) arguments on Yin-replenishing, and embraced a syncretistic approach to past medical teachings. Their clinical practice and most of the doctrinal debates in which they engaged were thus informed by the trends in medical thinking that I described in previous chapters. In the domain that interests us, the main event of the sixteenth century was perhaps the re-definition of dian 癲 as a form of madness characterized by non-manic symptoms and best treated by replenishing. The illness dian had existed since at least the third century BCE, and it had been associated with kuang since the first century BCE, but its main symptoms had first been close to those of epilepsy. When dian had been re-interpreted as a form of madness in the twelfth century, it had become so close to kuang in both etiology and symptoms that it could hardly be differentiated from kuang (3.4, 4.1). Dissatisfied with this confusion, many sixteenth-century physicians tried to reassert differences between dian and kuang. The clarifications proposed by a physician from Huizhou called Sun Yikui 孫一奎 (1522-1619) were eventually accepted by most elite physicians in the following centuries. They were Xu Xianqing 徐顯卿 (jinshi 1568, became Vice-Minister of Personnel, rank 3a) and Wu Shaoxi 吴少溪 (his hao), a former Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent (also ranked 3a). Theirs are cases 1, 4, 25, 29, 36, 37, 39, 40 of the Yixing 宜興 section of Sun's collection (Sunshi yian 孫氏醫案, juan 5). In 1597, Xu Xianqing wrote a preface to Sun's Chishui xuanzhu 赤水玄珠 (SunYQ: 4) soon after he had been cured by Sun, whom he had met almost two decades earlier (see cases 1 [1579], 29 [undated], 36 [1581], and 39 [1598]; in SunYQ: 827-28, 833A, 834-35, and 836AB). Sun also treated magistrate Hu Jingyang 胡鏡陽 and his family members (cases 5, 7, and 35; in SunYQ: 828B-29A, 829B, and 834A) and a magistrate surnamed Song 宋 from Shandong (case 3; SunYQ: 828B). $ ^{93} $ Sun went to Yixing from Huzhou in late 1597 and in the spring of 1598, and returned directly to Huzhou (which he called Tiao 苕 after the name of a local river). Late 1597 visit and return to Huzhou soon after the New Year: Yixing, case 37 (SunYQ: 835); arrival in the spring of 1598: case 2 (828); presence in Yixing in the late summer 1598: cases 39 and 40 (836-7); return to Huzhou in the fall of 1598: case 38 (835-6). Cases 1 and 2 (dated 1574), and case 3 (1577) in the San-Wu section (SunYQ: 735-36) show that Sun was in Huzhou in the 1570's.

Wang Wenbi's 汪文壁 preface to Sun's casebook (SunYQ: 709) explained that it was Huzhou gentry who had encouraged Sun to print his case files in a joint edition with Sun's two other books, (discussed below). Four of the five "Texts bestowed by illustrious local gentry" (諸縉紳名家贈文; SunYQ: 714-18) that appeared at the beginning of Sun's case collection were authored by Huzhou men, who called their native place Gui'an 歸安, Wuxing 吳興, or Xi Wu 西吳. The three dated texts were from 1573 (1) and 1576 (2). The 1573 text by Grand Coordinator (大中丞; ranked 2a) Shen Tong 沈桐 mentioned that Sun, who already enjoyed a good reputation at the time, was then beginning to travel in Huzhou (SunYQ: 716). Sun's collection is often dated to 1573 on the basis of its earliest "preface" (xu序), but the book's earliest dated case is from 1574, and I mentioned cases from 1598 in the previous note. The texts bestowed by Huzhou notables did not mention any book by Sun. A xu could indeed commemorate an occasion regardless of whether a book was being published.
I borrow my translation of the book's title from Zeitlin 2007.

$ ^{96} $ Xuyu 緒餘 referred to the unusable material that remained when silk thread had been pulled from a cocoon. A preface by his disciple Cheng Juan 程涓 commented that for someone so well versed in medicine to choose such a title was a case of great humility (謙讓未遑) (SunYQ: 643). Sun Yikui's nephew Sun Ye 燁 agreed.; arguing that medicine was considered a “minor Dao” because physicians themselves belittled it (醫道之小業醫者自小之也), he cited Sun's book title as an extreme example of this tendency (second preface [undated] to Yizhi xuyu 醫旨緒餘, SunYQ: 642).
